newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Reserves spur hunger for S.African shares, bonds.
newsitem.headline: Reserves spur hunger for S.African shares, bonds.

text.p: South African institutions returned as strong buyers of shares and bonds on Tuesday, heartened by a surge in official reserves, seen providing a buffer against the next easing in foreign exchange controls.

Analysts said that the massive jump in May gold and foreign exchange reserves had lowered portfolio managers' concerns on big cash outflows after July 1, when individuals will be allowed to invest limited amounts offshore.
Talk of a reduction in interest rates, possibly as early as the third quarter, had also flared up again in the stock market smoothing worries on recent poor company earnings reports.
"Things are looking up," said Willi Jonker, executive director of portfolio management, Norwich Investments.
"Although concerns remain over lower earnings from corporates in an environment of slower economic growth, that concern is outweighed by a better interest rate outlook," he said.

On Tuesday industrial equities climbed 60.0 points to a peak of 8,350.4, their highest level since May 22, before retracing to stand 46.4 higher by the close. Long bond yields fell to a best of 14.66 percent from 14.85 late on Monday, helped also by technical factors, before ending at 14.685.

Figures released late on Monday show South Africa's official reserves soared 51 percent to a record high of 21.8 billion rand ($4.9 billion) in May, streets ahead of the consensus forecast of 17.7 billion.

The 7.4 billion rand month-on-month improvement, boosted by inflows from the privatisation of telecommunications concern Telkom, lifts the country's import cover to more than two months for the first time since the rand crisis broke early last year.
"Portfolio managers have been sitting long of cash waiting for July 1 to pass. But with the reserves it looks like there won't be a problem," a dealer said.
The size of the investments which private individuals will be allowed to make offshore has not yet been announced.

Sentiment on interest rates has see-sawed in the last week. A rise in inflation to a 22-month high of 9.9 percent in April initially damped down hopes but a shock slide in first quarter gross domestic product later revived them.
"Suddenly market views on interest rates seem to have changed again, people are now again talking of them coming down soon," a dealer said.

Reserve Bank governor Chris Stals has indicated, however, he not going to act precipatedly -- and many economists believe he will not loosen monetary policy until he is able to assess the impact of the July 1 exchange control relaxation.
